# App Audio Router

> Free, open-source per-app audio routing for Windows 10 / 11 (64-bit): send one program's audio to several playback devices at once, each with its own signed-millisecond delay compensation and its own 0–100 % volume balance. Built as a single native binary on the Windows Core Audio API — no virtual audio driver, no helper executable, nothing left behind on uninstall. MIT licensed, version %APP_VERSION%, interface in English and Simplified Chinese.

Key facts, all from the project documentation. Each line stands on its own:

- App Audio Router is a per-application audio router for Windows. Windows itself lets an application play to only one output at a time; this app lifts that restriction.
- One application → many playback devices simultaneously. The first device is the native Windows endpoint; every further device receives a real-time mirrored copy of the stream via WASAPI process loopback.
- Routing applies to already-running programs immediately — no restart. A game or a browser tab keeps playing while its sound moves to the new devices.
- Stopping a route hands the program back to the system default device. While a route is live, Windows stores a fixed output device for that program (the mechanism that moves a running program's audio), and it outranks the system default; stopping the route, quitting the app, and **Settings → Reset per-app output** each release it. Releasing needs the program to be running, because the audio service is addressed by process.
- Per-device delay compensation is a signed millisecond value: positive holds a fast device back, negative marks the earliest device in the route. It aligns wired speakers with a Bluetooth headset — a typical Bluetooth offset is about +180 ms.
- Delay can only *add* latency. The earliest device of the group is the alignment reference and cannot be pulled earlier, which is why routing is applied in delay order.
- Per-device volume balance is 0–100 % and can only attenuate, relative to the loudest device in the route. Changes are pushed to live routes and are audible immediately.
- Mirrored copies are buffered for stability (about 100 ms of pipeline latency) so every mirrored device plays the same sample at the same moment. Alignment between mirrored devices is exact; the offset to the primary device, which Windows plays natively, is inherent to capturing and re-rendering the stream.
- Routing rules are remembered per executable name — not per path or PID — and restored automatically the next time that program plays.
- The app never polls and runs no service: it registers for the audio engine's own change notifications, so the device and process lists stay current by themselves.
- It is tray-resident, with optional close-to-tray and optional start-with-Windows (a single `HKCU\...\Run` value for the current user; no administrator rights, nothing written to `HKLM`).
- Routes for system-critical processes are refused rather than half-applied.
- Windows-only (Windows 10 / 11, 64-bit). Not available on macOS or Linux.

## What it cannot do

- It cannot make a program appear in the process list before that program holds an active audio session; a program only shows up while it is producing sound.
- It cannot route programs that use ASIO or WASAPI exclusive mode: those never create a session with the system audio engine, so they are invisible to any per-app router.
- It cannot speed a device up (delay only adds) or make a device louder than the application's own level (volume only attenuates).
- It cannot release the fixed output device of a program that is not running; a closed program keeps its device until it plays again.
- It runs on Windows only — the routing mechanism is the Windows Core Audio API.

## Quick answers

**Is App Audio Router free?** Yes. Open source under the MIT licence, with no paid tier and no account.

**Does it need a virtual audio driver such as VB-CABLE?** No. Routing, duplication, delay and gain are all done by the app itself, calling the Windows Core Audio API directly. Nothing is installed into the audio stack, and uninstalling leaves no driver behind.

**Can it change the output of a program that is already running?** Yes. Routing applies to the live audio session, so the program does not need to be restarted.

**After stopping a route, does the program follow the system default device again?** Yes — that is the point of version 2.1.1. Versions before 2.1.1 left the device fixed after a stop, which is why a program could keep playing to the old device, or ignore the system's device switches, until the reset was done.

**Why is a program missing from the list?** It has no active audio session (start playback, or press Refresh), it uses ASIO / WASAPI exclusive mode, or it is a system-critical process, which is deliberately excluded.

**Can it fix the desync between a Bluetooth headset and wired speakers?** Yes, that is what delay compensation is for: give the faster device the Bluetooth device's lag as a positive delay, for example +180 ms.

**Is macOS or Linux supported?** No. Windows 10 and 11, 64-bit only.

## Specifications

| | |
|---|---|
| Name | App Audio Router (AAR) |
| Version | %APP_VERSION% |
| Platform | Windows 10 / Windows 11, 64-bit |
| Runtime requirement | WebView2 Runtime — bundled with Windows 11, present on any Windows 10 with Microsoft Edge |
| External dependencies | None: no virtual audio driver, no service, no third-party executable |
| Installer | MSI or NSIS setup from GitHub Releases |
| Licence | MIT |
| Interface languages | English, Simplified Chinese |
| Built with | Tauri 2, Rust, React 19, TypeScript, TailwindCSS, Vite |
| Settings storage | Plain JSON in the app data directory: `route-memory.json`, `device-delays.json`, `device-volumes.json`, `app-settings.json`, `install-state.json` |
